transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Aurelius CTO), Samir Patel (Infra), Rachel Kim (Security)

Summary (auto):
Redwood and Aurelius dug into Private VPC networking options for a private deployment. Focus on PrivateLink vs NAT egress, subnet sizing, DNS resolution (split-horizon / Route53), ENI limits, cross-account endpoints, and how networking choices affect runtime latency, KV cache locality, and batching behavior. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send architecture doc+PrivateLink gallery, Aurelius to share VPC CIDR/quotas, schedule pilot for quantized model benchmarking.

Topics:
- PrivateLink vs NAT egress cost and latency tradeoffs
- Subnet and AZ placement for inference workers and KV cache
- DNS (split-horizon, resolver IPs, Route53 private hosted zones)
- ENI and IP exhaustion, scaling considerations
- Batching and KV cache TTL/eviction behavior across endpoints
- Security: cross-account policies, VPC endpoints, flow logs, KMS/HSM for keys

Action items (brief): see metadata section below.

Transcript:
[00:00] Michael Chen (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Lena Ortiz (Aurelius): Lena here.
[00:07] Samir Patel (Aurelius): Samir here.
[00:09] Rachel Kim (Aurelius): Rachel here.
[00:11] Priya Kapoor (Redwood): Priya here.
[00:12] Michael Chen: Cool. We'll jump in — goal is to map networking patterns for Private VPC deploy and how those choices impact runtime perf, latency, KV cache locality, and cost.

[02:01] Priya Kapoor: Quick overview: Redwood Private installs a customer-managed control plane in your account (or cross-account) and can be deployed in two main networking patterns: 1) PrivateLink-style interface endpoints where the control plane talks via AWS Interface VPC endpoints (so no internet egress) and 2) NAT-egress model where we use NAT Gateway/egress but keep endpoints private via IP allowlists. Both have pros/cons.

[03:10] Samir Patel: Can you describe differences in latency between PrivateLink vs NAT? We're very latency sensitive (p95 generation target < 200ms).

[03:25] Priya Kapoor: Sure. PrivateLink typically reduces jitter because traffic stays within the AWS network and hits ENIs in the service VPC directly, so you avoid internet path variability. If you're using NAT gateway and endpoints traverse the public internet (even with TLS), you can see higher variance and extra egress hop; plus NAT adds a small ms overhead and potential burst costs. That said, PrivateLink requires ENI capacity and cross-account endpoint setup.

[05:00] Michael Chen: Also important is where the model runtime lives relative to the KV cache. If the KV cache (prefix/KV cache for transformer KV) is co-located within same VPC/subnet (or attached via high-bandwidth ENI), you get local KV hits with <1ms extra hop; cross-VPC calls add tens of ms depending on path. So we recommend colocating compute and cache.

[06:10] Lena Ortiz: We're planning to keep inference on dedicated GPU nodes in our VPC. We were hoping to avoid lots of ENIs — what's the ENI limit per AZ and how does Redwood recommend scaling?

[06:40] Priya Kapoor: ENI limits depend on instance type and account limits. For large GPU instances, ENI per instance can be limited; also AWS account-level ENI quotas can bite if you have many pods/instances. Typical patterns: place inference nodes in multiple private subnets across AZs, reserve a pool of warm instances, or use fewer larger instances with multi-tenant workers. We'll share our sizing guidelines.

[08:20] Samir Patel: What about IP exhaustion — we already have limited CIDR ranges. Can we use smaller subnets?

[08:45] Priya Kapoor: Yes, but watch overall IP availability. Options: use NAT with centralized egress to reduce number of public IPs, use AWS PrivateLink to avoid public IPs for endpoints, or use VPC Peering/Transit Gateway if you want cross-account private connectivity. Each has tradeoffs: Transit Gateway is powerful but costs more and can add a bit of latency.

[10:05] Rachel Kim: From security perspective we prefer no internet egress for model inference traffic. PrivateLink sounds good but need to confirm cross-account IAM & policy boundaries. Also need flow logs and auditability.

[10:30] Priya Kapoor: We support VPC endpoint policies for PrivateLink, and we can run the control plane cross-account or within your account as a customer-managed deployment to satisfy audit demands. Flow logs, VPC Flow Logs, and SG rules are supported; we can integrate with your logging pipeline. We'll also supply SOC2 artifacts for enterprise customers.

[12:00] Michael Chen: Let's talk DNS — split-horizon Route53 private hosted zone vs custom DNS resolver. How do you typically resolve Redwood API hostnames in PrivateLink?

[12:25] Priya Kapoor: Two options: 1) We publish an interface endpoint DNS name that resolves to the ENI private IPs — you can use AWS's provided private DNS for interface endpoints or create a private hosted zone with the same FQDN pointing to the endpoint IPs, or 2) use resolver rules to forward specific domains to our resolver. Split-horizon is common if you want same hostname public vs private. Caveat: if you change endpoints (scaling), the IPs may rotate, so you want the endpoint abstraction instead of hard-coding IPs.

[14:10] Samir Patel: Will we need to touch Route53 records every time you scale? That would be painful.

[14:25] Priya Kapoor: No — with AWS interface endpoints + private DNS enabled, DNS for the service domain is handled automatically, no manual updates needed. If you prefer private hosted zones we can provide automation scripts / CloudFormation to keep records in sync.

[16:00] Lena Ortiz: How does this impact KV cache — if the runtime scales out into multiple AZs, do we risk cache misses because KV cache is per-AZ?

[16:20] Priya Kapoor: Good question. Our runtime has a local in-memory KV cache per worker process to accelerate autoregressive generation token reuse (prefix caching). Cache hit rates depend on request routing: if routing pins a session to same worker or same AZ where a shared cache tier exists, hit rates are higher. For cross-AZ calls you can add a shared cache tier (Redis/Memcached) accessible over the VPC — but that adds a network hop and affects p95. We recommend colocating a small cache cluster within each AZ or sticky routing for sessions.

[18:05] Michael Chen: Also quantization affects memory footprint and KV cache size — 8-bit quant reduces KV memory per layer so you can store more in worker memory, reducing cross-node cache pressure. But quantization sometimes increases compute latency slightly depending on kernels. We'll show benchmark numbers.

[19:40] Samir Patel: Would you recommend dedicated subnets for the Redwood workers and another for cache?

[19:55] Priya Kapoor: Yes. Typical pattern: private subnets per AZ for Redwood inference workers, private subnets for cache nodes (Redis) in same AZs, and a management subnet for control-plane ENIs/PrivateLink. Put load balancers or interface endpoints in a separate subnet if you want strict SG segmentation.

[21:30] Rachel Kim: On encryption — we must keep keys in our KMS/HSM. Does Redwood support customer-managed CMKs for data at rest and in-transit key exchange?

[21:50] Michael Chen: Yes — for Private deployments we can integrate with your KMS. We also support key wrapping and customer-managed HSM if needed; we'll include the security integration doc.

[23:30] Priya Kapoor: One more networking wrinkle: when using PrivateLink cross-account, you'll create interface endpoints in your account which create ENIs that talk to our service. If you plan to use cross-AZ scaling and have lots of endpoints, consider ENI quota increases and also ensure SG/Egress rules allow high throughput between nodes.

[25:10] Samir Patel: What about NAT costs — our finance team is worried about NAT data egress pricing if we go NAT route.

[25:25] Michael Chen: NAT costs can add up for heavy token egress. PrivateLink avoids NAT egress charges because traffic stays within the AWS backbone. If you do require egress (e.g., callouts to external APIs), you can centralize and use egress proxies to control costs, but for Redwood inference traffic PrivateLink is the cost-favorable option in many cases. We'll put a cost comparison spreadsheet in the follow-up.

[27:40] Priya Kapoor: Also consider using VPC endpoints for S3/Secrets Manager so model artifacts and keys don't need internet egress. That keeps the whole pipeline internal.

[29:00] Lena Ortiz: Any differences for on-prem or hybrid setups? We might run edge inference on-prem in future.

[29:20] Priya Kapoor: For on-prem we support private deployment with VPN or Direct Connect to the control plane; for data plane you can run the runtime on-prem and connect back to control plane over private link/peering. Latency is obviously higher depends on dedicate link; for high throughput on-prem, we recommend colocating both control and data plane components.

[31:10] Michael Chen: Real-world note: customers who tried a single centralized KV cache across AZs saw p95 regression from ~120ms to ~220ms when cross-AZ misses increased. Local cache per AZ or sticky routing recovered p95 to sub-150ms. We'll attach those benchmark traces.

[33:05] Samir Patel: Can we do sticky routing? How deterministic is session pinning?

[33:20] Priya Kapoor: Yes — we support session affinity options in the routing layer: sticky by session id, consistent hashing by user id, or round-robin with warm pools. Sticky routing increases cache hit rates but reduces flexibility during scale-down/balance events — you can set TTL/affinity windows.

[35:00] Rachel Kim: For compliance we need audit logs of request IDs and keys used. Do you log tokens? We can't have raw PII or data logged.

[35:20] Michael Chen: We don't log full customer payloads by default; logging is configurable. For enterprise Private deployments we can disable sensitive payload logging and provide request metadata logs (IDs, latencies, errors) for auditing. We also support ingesting logs to your S3 or SIEM.

[37:00] Priya Kapoor: A small note on batching: batching increases throughput but adds queuing latency. Our runtime has adaptive batching tuned for latency SLOs — it will batch up to a configured max batch size and wait a short micro-window for coalescing. In Private VPC deployments, network latency is lower, so batching gains are more predictable. Quantization can influence per-token time, so we'll show combined batching+quantization benchmarks.

[39:20] Samir Patel: For the pilot, what do you need from us to run a benchmark?

[39:35] Priya Kapoor: We'll need VPC CIDR ranges, subnets per AZ, any firewall rules or proxy egress constraints, ENI quotas, and a test dataset (prompt set) plus desired SLOs (p50/p95 latency targets). Also an account or cross-account role for Redwood to deploy the control-plane resources or a CloudFormation template if you want to self-deploy.

[41:10] Michael Chen: We'll propose 3 scenarios: PrivateLink with per-AZ cache, NAT-egress with centralized cache, and PrivateLink + quantized model with sticky routing. We'll run 1k sample prompts at concurrent QPS targets to show p50/p95 and cost delta.

[43:00] Rachel Kim: Anything about DNS caching on clients that could cause stale endpoints? We have aggressive local resolver caches.

[43:20] Priya Kapoor: Yes — if you rely on DNS names that can change due to scaling, TTLs are important. With interface endpoints and AWS private DNS the records are stable; if you run own hosted zone set TTL low during testing, then increase. Also ensure your resolver forwards to VPC resolver so endpoint names resolve properly.

[45:05] Samir Patel: Are there recommendations for security groups for low-latency traffic?

[45:20] Priya Kapoor: Keep SG rules permissive within the inferencing subnets for the worker/cache communication on internal ports, but lock down egress to only required endpoints for external calls. Use SGs to limit access to the control-plane ENIs (PrivateLink).

[47:00] Michael Chen: A note on scale events: when we scale a pool quickly, we create ENIs and new worker processes — there can be a short period where DNS/SGs update and some flows retried. We aim for graceful warmup with a rolling scale-in to avoid cold cache storms.

[49:15] Lena Ortiz: For our timeline — we'd like pilot in ~2 weeks if possible. Is that realistic?

[49:30] Michael Chen: Yes, if you can provide VPC details and quota increases quickly. We'll start with architecture doc and a CloudFormation template for PrivateLink endpoints and the control-plane resources.

[51:00] Priya Kapoor: We'll also include an example of the endpoint policy and cross-account role trust policy — common pain point.

[52:10] Samir Patel: One last thing — are there any gotchas with IPv6?

[52:30] Priya Kapoor: Most customers use IPv4 for control plane traffic; IPv6 adds complexity with egress and NAT64. If you need IPv6 we can discuss, but plan for extra testing.

[54:00] Rachel Kim: Okay, sounds good. Can you recap next steps?

[54:10] Michael Chen: Recap: Redwood to send Private VPC architecture + PrivateLink gallery + cost comparison spreadsheet; Priya to share endpoint policy examples and cache sizing guide; Aurelius to supply VPC CIDRs, subnets, ENI quotas, and compliance artifact list. We'll schedule the pilot benchmark (target week of 11/18).

[55:20] Samir Patel: Thanks. We'll aim to turn around the CIDR info by Friday.

[55:30] Lena Ortiz: Thanks all.

[55:35] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and set up the pilot invite.

[56:00] (call ends)
